seo.title: Karmic tail 9 18 9 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 18 9 compatibility: why a couple's tail begins and ends with The Hermit, what The Moon hides in between, and what the couple has to learn.

title: The couple tail 9-18-9: one lighthouse, seen twice
short: The karmic tail 9-18-9 has an odd shape: it begins and ends with the same card. The Hermit stands both at the entry to the task and at the main task, with The Moon between them. The answer to the riddle is that this is one and the same Hermit, seen from two distances. At the entry he is what the couple wants together: quiet for two, a solitude of one's own for each, understanding without words. In the middle that quiet fills up with guesses. At the main task the same Hermit turns into two separate solitudes, and what the couple has to learn is not a love of quiet — it already has that — but the knack of stepping out of its own quiet towards the other in time.

sections.h2: A novel in which the most important things are never said aloud
paragraphs: In 1927 Virginia Woolf published To the Lighthouse. Almost nothing happens in it. The Ramsay family is staying in its summer house on the Isle of Skye. The youngest son, James, longs to sail to the lighthouse; his mother promises, "Yes, of course, if it's fine tomorrow"; his father says it will not be fine. The trip is put off for ten years. Everything else is what people think while they talk about something else.

Mr and Mrs Ramsay are a couple in whom the 9-18-9 tail is recognisable at once. He is a philosopher over sixty; she is a beautiful woman of fifty, the mother of eight. They love each other and almost never say so. Woolf drew them from her own parents. Later she admitted that until the novel was written her mother would not let her go: "I could hear her voice, see her." More about that admission at the end: it is the way out of the tail.

Even the shape of the book repeats the tail. The novel has three parts: "The Window", "Time Passes" and "The Lighthouse". In the first, the lighthouse is seen from afar, from the drawing-room window. In the second, night falls: the house stands empty, the lamps go out, and the lighthouse beam wanders through the rooms mixed with moonlight. In the third, they finally sail out and see the lighthouse up close. Lighthouse — twilight — lighthouse again: 9-18-9.
Quotations from the novel below are given in Woolf's own words.

sections.h2: Waite's clue: the Hermit's lantern is called a beacon
paragraphs: The first clue is in Waite's English text. Describing his Hermit card, he twice calls the lantern a beacon. The figure is "holding up his beacon on an eminence". And then: "His beacon intimates that 'where I am, you also may be.'" A beacon is a signal fire on a height, a lighthouse for those in the dark. Benebell Wen uses the same word: a person under this card can be "the mentor or beacon of wisdom for others". Her Hermit "stands on snowy peaks".

In Woolf the lighthouse is the Hermit on the scale of the sea: a single light on a bare rock. And the lighthouse keeper appears in the very first chapter. Mrs Ramsay is knitting a stocking for his little boy, and she explains to her daughters why the keeper should be sent a parcel: how would you like to be "shut up for a whole month at a time, and possibly more in stormy weather, upon a rock the size of a tennis lawn… to see nobody; if you were married, not to see your wife". The whole novel is about getting a parcel to a hermit.

And the Ramsays themselves are two hermits of different make. Of him Woolf writes that he comes out "on a spit of land which the sea is slowly eating away, and there to stand, like a desolate sea-bird, alone", "on his little ledge facing the dark of human ignorance". It is almost the image Waite describes on his card: a lone figure on an eminence. She withdraws differently. When the children are in bed she needs only one thing: "To be silent; to be alone." Then she becomes "a wedge-shaped core of darkness, something invisible to others", and looks at the lighthouse — at "the long steady stroke, the last of the three, which was her stroke". One stands facing the dark; the other becomes the darkness that looks at the light. In this couple The Hermit and The Moon are not shared out between the two people: both cards live in both.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "Don't interrupt. Just sit there"
paragraphs: The key scene of the tail is one evening, chapter nineteen of the first part. Mrs Ramsay comes into the room where her husband is reading Sir Walter Scott. She sits down in her particular chair under her particular lamp, takes up her knitting, then a book of poems. He does not want to be interrupted — that is clear. And this is not a grievance; it is their common language:

Their eyes met for a second; but they did not want to speak to each other. They had nothing to say, but something seemed, nevertheless, to go from him to her. […] Don't interrupt me, he seemed to be saying, don't say anything; just sit there.

A little later he thinks about her: "He liked to think that every one had taken themselves off and that he and she were alone." Here is the couple's wish at the entry to the task. Not a celebration and not a passion — a room where two people are silent together and content. In Lisovskaya's book this nine looks like this: each has a time and a place for solitude, love is shown by deeds rather than words, there is trust and there are shared agreements. Mrs Ramsay guards his quiet. In the daytime, when he paces the terrace "as if he wrapped himself about and needed privacy into which to regain his equilibrium", "not for the world would she have spoken to him".

On the site this nine appears twice for the couple. Point M is not only the "Entry to the task" of the tail but also the "Common language" in the sphere "Relationship and common language". For a 9-18-9 couple The Hermit literally is the common language.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can turn into resistance. The agreement not to disturb works while both need quiet. In the same scene, a little later, Mrs Ramsay needs something quite different: "Do say something, she thought, wishing only to hear his voice… Say anything, she begged, looking at him". Aloud — not a word. By the rules of their common language, one does not interrupt.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the crepuscular walls of intimacy
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle of the tail no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. Here it is read as the couple's path — what the two live through between the wish and the task. For 9-18-9 that path runs through The Moon, and Woolf describes it in words that could hardly be bettered: the two sit "drawing together, involuntarily, coming side by side", and she feels his mind "through the crepuscular walls of their intimacy". The shadow, "the thing folding them in", is beginning to close round her again.

What happens in the twilight? Each lives beside a partner they have partly drawn in themselves. Mr Ramsay watches his wife reading and "exaggerated her ignorance, her simplicity, for he liked to think that she was not clever, not book-learned at all. He wondered if she understood what she was reading. Probably not, he thought." And she has just climbed a Shakespeare sonnet "on to the top, on to the summit" and holds it in her hands, "beautiful and reasonable, clear and complete". He sees a simple woman; she is standing on the summit. In Woolf, The Moon is not a deception but a portrait of the partner painted in poor light.

Mrs Ramsay fills in the picture too. Going over the evening's events, she recalls a guest "waking them with his books falling — oh, no, that she had invented". The invented thing has settled in memory next to the real ones, and she barely notices the seam.

And in the twilight small things pile up. Woolf names them one by one: Mrs Ramsay is "not being able to tell him the truth". She is afraid to say that mending the greenhouse roof will cost "fifty pounds perhaps". She is afraid "that he might guess, what she a little suspected, that his last book was not quite his best book". She has "to hide small daily things, and the children seeing it, and the burden it laid on them". No dreadful secrets: a bill for the greenhouse and an honest opinion of a book. This is how The Moon grows in a quiet couple — not out of lies but out of the unsaid. In Lisovskaya, the minus of The Moon includes hidden feelings, fear, and grievances that are more often imagined than real. The Ramsays have all of this, only in miniature.

paragraphs.h3: The Moon speaks in borrowed words

paragraphs: Wen has a sentence that explains this couple better than any other: "Key 18 represents poetry and mystery." And the Ramsays really do speak in poems — other people's. Sitting next to her husband, she reads Shakespeare's Sonnet 98 about absence: "Yet seem'd it winter still, and, you away, / As with your shadow I with these did play". Lines about someone who is not there — two steps away from him. He, meanwhile, weeps over a Scott novel, "raising the book a little to hide his face".

At dinner her husband recites the poem "Luriana Lurilee", and to Mrs Ramsay "the words seemed to be spoken by her own voice, outside her self, saying quite easily and naturally what had been in her mind the whole evening while she said different things". This is the double nature of The Moon in a couple. On its plus side, Lisovskaya says such couples understand each other from half a word, or intuitively. On its minus side, they hide their feelings and treat tender words as weakness. With the Ramsays both sides work on the same evening.

The evening ends like this. Her husband remarks: "You won't finish that stocking tonight." "No," she says, "I shan't finish it." It is the very stocking for the lighthouse keeper's son. She has been knitting it since the first chapter, and on this evening it stays unfinished. And then comes the main thing:

He wanted something—wanted the thing she always found it so difficult to give him; wanted her to tell him that she loved him. And that, no, she could not do. […] A heartless woman he called her; she never told him that she loved him. But it was not so—it was not so. It was only that she never could say what she felt.

He thinks: "Will you not tell me just for once that you love me?" She gets up, goes to the window, turns, smiles — and says: "Yes, you were right. It's going to be wet tomorrow. You won't be able to go." The last line of the chapter: **"She had not said it: yet he knew."**

Here is the main task of 9-18-9 in a single line. Woolf calls it a triumph: "she had triumphed again". And it truly is the plus of the tail — understanding without words, the thing the couple entered the task for. But the same line holds the minus. The word is never said, and more than once he has called her silence heartless. Lisovskaya gives The Moon a piece of advice that fits this scene word for word: accept that a partner sometimes needs to sink into themselves; it does not mean they do not love you — this is how they recover their strength. Mr Ramsay read his wife's quiet as lack of love — a mistake made in the twilight.

The scene shows what each of them is waiting for. All evening she silently asks: "Say anything." He silently asks: "Just for once." Two silences, each waiting for the first word from the other. This is what The Hermit looks like at the main task. Lisovskaya lists it: each partner is on their own, problems are not voiced but stored up inside, and from outside the partners seem cold, as if from another planet. And the couple's tasks: not to hide in one's shell when trouble comes, to share and to listen in return, to feel for the line between supporting someone and simply leaving them alone.

The novel shows the price too. In the third part, ten years on, Mr Ramsay does take the children to the lighthouse. They sail in silence, having vowed to each other "to resist tyranny to the death": "Speak to him they could not." Silence has become the family's language. In the daughter's head a line keeps turning, the one her father keeps repeating — from William Cowper's poem The Castaway (1799): "We perished, each alone." The same stanza of Cowper's says: "No light propitious shone". This is The Hermit's shadow: not a lantern on the summit but solitude without a light.

On the very day the novel opens, Mrs Ramsay had been reading her son the Grimms' tale The Fisherman and His Wife — the one Pushkin turned into his Tale of the Fisherman and the Fish. Woolf weaves it through the novel "like the bass gently accompanying a tune". Once more the wife sends the fisherman to the sea, and Woolf quotes: "He said to himself, 'It is not right,' and yet he went." Pushkin puts it more briefly: "The old man dared not contradict her, / Dared not say a word against her" (our translation). The tale, too, is about the main task of this tail: the truth is told to oneself, not to the one beside you.

sections.h2: "Nothing was simply one thing": why The Hermit stands twice
paragraphs: The most precise sentence about a palindrome tail is also in Woolf. In the third part James, now sixteen, sails up to the lighthouse and sees it close: "the tower, stark and straight", "barred with black and white", windows, and "washing spread on the rocks to dry". Before, in childhood, the lighthouse was "a silvery, misty-looking tower with a yellow eye, that opened suddenly, and softly in the evening". And James thinks:
So that was the Lighthouse, was it? No, the other was also the Lighthouse. For nothing was simply one thing.

This is the answer to why the tail has two nines. **The Hermit at the entry is the lighthouse seen from the window**: a lovely misty dream of quiet for two. **The Hermit at the main task is the same lighthouse up close**: a striped tower, washing on the rocks, solitude as daily work with a price of its own. The Moon between them is the night and the distance across the bay. The card does not change. The distance does, and the couple's task is not to swap its card for another but to sail up to it.

Wen offers a hint for telling the two Hermits apart. She writes: "There are two ways of interpreting the lighted lantern. Some suggest that it represents wisdom and the shining of light in the darkness for others. Another is to interpret the lighted lantern as representing someone who sees the world through his or her own light." The Hermit "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only". In the 9-18-9 tail both readings stand side by side. At the entry each is a beacon for the other: where I am, you also may be. At the main task each sees the other only by their own lamp. That is how Mr Ramsay sees a simple woman in his wife.

From outside the two Hermits cannot be told apart. In the boat near the lighthouse Mr Ramsay looks at the island in silence, and the children wonder: "he might be thinking, We perished, each alone, or he might be thinking, I have reached it. I have found it; but he said nothing." The same silence can be defeat or victory, and the other person can tell which only from words. "They both wanted to say, Ask us anything and we will give it you. But he did not ask them anything."

sections.h2: The green shawl: the way out of the 9-18-9 tail
paragraphs: Woolf showed the way out too — earlier, in the middle of the first part. Mr Ramsay passes the window and sees his wife: she is alone, lost in thought and, it seems, sad. He wants urgently to speak to her.

But he resolved, no; he would not interrupt her. […] He would let her be, and he passed her without a word, though it hurt him that she should look so distant, and he could not reach her, he could do nothing to help her. And again he would have passed her without a word had she not, at that very moment, given him of her own free will what she knew he would never ask, and called to him and taken the green shawl off the picture frame, and gone to him. For he wished, she knew, to protect her.

In this paragraph the tail is worked through correctly, from the first point to the last. He respects her solitude — that is the entry. She guesses his wish — The Moon, which this time does not mislead. And she steps out of her own quiet first, unasked — that is the main task solved. The line Lisovskaya writes about, between supporting and leaving alone, is crossed here from both sides. He chose to leave her be; she chose to come to him. Neither of them is wrong. All that matters is that someone stepped out.

Ten years later, in the boat, Mr Ramsay says one word to his son. James has steered them "like a born sailor", and his father says: "Well done!" His sister says to him silently: "You've got it at last." She knew "that this was what James had been wanting". The way out of the tail can be just as small. Not a confession and not a showdown, but one word said aloud, one of those the other "knows anyway".
What this means for a couple, translating the novel into everyday life:

ul: **Say what kind of quiet it is.** "I need some time alone — it's not about you" tells the two Hermits apart: from outside, the lighthouse from the window and solitude without a light look the same.
**Check guesses with a question.** The Moon fills in the partner in poor light. A short "are you tired or angry?" is worth more than an evening of silent conclusions.
**Name small things while they are still small.** A greenhouse bill and an honest opinion of a book turn into walls only when they are hidden for a long time.
**Sometimes step out first, without waiting to be asked.** The green shawl is taken off without asking whether it is wanted.
**Say simple things aloud.** "I love you", "well done", "I'm here" — exactly what the other has long known. Knowing and hearing are different things.

paragraphs: Woolf herself went down this road — on her parents' behalf. When the novel was finished, she wrote: "I wrote the book very quickly; and when it was written, I ceased to be obsessed by my mother. I no longer hear her voice; I do not see her. […] I expressed some very long felt and deeply felt emotion. And in expressing it I explained it and then laid it to rest." The novel needed ten years and an empty house for the unsaid to be heard. A couple with the 9-18-9 tail needs only one evening.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: how the 9-18-9 tail adds up
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The 9-18-9 tail occurs in about one couple in 88 (1.136%) and ranks 31st of the 97 couple tails. It comes from six combinations of personal tails, and the three main ones say a lot:

ul: **18-6-6 + 9-12-3 — 49% of such couples.** The Moon in the middle is built from The Lovers and The Hanged Man: 6 + 12. The couple's twilight is born of love and waiting.
**18-9-9 + 9-9-18 — 31%.** Each partner has a Hermit in the middle, and two Hermits make The Moon: 9 + 9 = 18.
**15-8-11 + 21-10-16 — 11%.** Neither partner has The Hermit or The Moon in their personal tail. The couple does not bring the quiet and the twilight with it — they are born only between the two.

paragraphs: Our own run over all dates with the site's engine adds a detail: in 80% of such couples a nine or an eighteen appears in the personal tails of both partners, and in 20% in neither. It never happens that only one partner has these cards. There is no single "hermit" paired with an ordinary person: the couple holds the quiet together, and both will have to step out of it.

The clue in the centre is stronger still. The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere, what is between the two when nobody is watching. In 81.3% of 9-18-9 couples The Moon stands there; in the remaining 18.7%, The Hermit. Woolf's "crepuscular walls of their intimacy" are not just a stage on the path. For most such couples twilight is the very atmosphere of the union. In "The couple's values" The Hermit stands in 75.1% and The Moon in 24.9%. No other cards ever appear in these two points for 9-18-9: the core of the couple is written in two arcana only. Most often (60.2%) it is The Moon in the centre and The Hermit in the values. The union breathes twilight and rests on each partner's right to their own depth.

And one last coincidence. In the most frequent combination (49%), the couple's centre and the middle of its tail are built from the same numbers, crosswise. The partner with the personal tail 18-6-6 has a centre of 12 and a tail middle of 6. The partner with 9-12-3 has it the other way round: centre 6, middle 12. What lies at the core of one lies halfway along the path of the other. That is why the couple's Moon appears twice: 6 + 12 in the centre and 12 + 6 in the middle of the tail.
The first partner's personal tail is 9-12-3, the second's is 18-6-6. The couple's tail adds up point by point:

The couple's centre is The Moon too: 6 + 12 = 18, the same "crosswise". "The couple's values" are recalculated from the couple's own sums and give The Hermit, 9. In the reading the entry nine appears once more, in the sphere "Relationship and common language", captioned "Common language". Five times in the couple's main places — the same two cards.

sections.h2: 9-18-9, 9-9-18 and 18-9-9: the same cards in another order
paragraphs: The same numbers make two more couple tails. In **9-9-18** (3.26% of couples) The Moon stands at the main task: the couple's difficulty is the fog itself. It has to make out the real partner behind an image that formed during a long silence. In **18-9-9** (1.754% of couples) the couple enters through The Moon — through mystery and enchantment — and then passes The Hermit twice. Its task is to learn to share solitude. In 9-18-9 the fog is only the path, and the task is the quiet itself: not to fall out of love with it, but to learn to step out of it towards the other.
The same order 9-18-9 also occurs as a personal karmic tail, in one person's chart. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and it has an article of its own.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** The couple's common language is silence side by side. The two are happy together without words and guard each other's solitude. This is both the way in and the resistance: "don't disturb me" easily becomes "don't speak".
**N · Middle of the task — 18, The Moon.** The path runs through twilight. What goes unsaid piles up, and its place is taken by guesses, fears and other people's words — poems, books, hints.

**D · Main task — 9, The Hermit.** The same quiet, on its minus side: each lives on their own, troubles pile up in silence. The lesson is to sense when to leave the other alone and when to come over first, and to say aloud what the other "knows anyway".

intro: This is not a verdict or a forecast: the tail describes how a couple works through its main task, not what will happen to it. To see that task whole, one needs a story in which such a couple has already been described. There is one — and it is described down to a single evening.

faq.q: Is the 9-18-9 tail a bad sign for compatibility?
faq.a: No. The tail does not grade the union and does not foretell events. It shows the couple's main task. For 9-18-9 that task grows out of a strength: the two are happy together in quiet and can understand each other without words. The difficulty begins where understanding without words replaces words altogether.

faq.q: Does 9-18-9 mean the couple will drift apart?
faq.a: No. The Hermit at the main task is not a fate but a theme on which the couple learns: when to leave each other alone and when to come over first. The task is solved not by giving up quiet but by talking about it: what kind of quiet it is right now, and what it is for.

faq.q: Who in the couple is The Hermit, and who is The Moon?
faq.a: Neither. A couple's tail is built from two personal matrices, and its cards belong to the couple, not to one of the partners. In 80% of such couples a nine or an eighteen appears in both partners' personal tails, in 20% in neither. It never happens that only one partner has these cards. The quiet is held by two, and nobody is to blame for it.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 9-18-9 differ from the personal one?
faq.a: A personal 9-18-9 tail describes one person, and its points have roles of their own. A couple's tail is added up from the same points of two matrices and is read as shared tasks: M is the entry to the task and the common language, N is the middle of the path, D is the couple's main task. Readings cannot be carried from one to the other, even when the numbers are the same.

report: In Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse a husband waits all evening for three words from his wife, and she talks to him about the weather — and wins. "She had not said it: yet he knew," the chapter ends. That one line holds the whole 9-18-9 tail: both what the couple does better than others and what it still has to learn.

The oddity of the tail is plain at once: it begins and ends with the same card. The Hermit stands at the entry to the task and at the main task, with The Moon between them. Describing his Hermit, Waite twice calls the lantern a beacon: the figure is "holding up his beacon on an eminence". And Woolf has a sentence that explains why the lighthouse should stand in the tail twice. James, now sixteen, sails up to the lighthouse and sees a tower "stark and straight", "barred with black and white", with "washing spread on the rocks to dry". In his childhood it was "a silvery, misty-looking tower with a yellow eye". And James thinks:
So that was the Lighthouse, was it? No, the other was also the Lighthouse. For nothing was simply one thing.

**The Hermit at the entry is the lighthouse seen from the window**: a dream of quiet for two. A couple with this tail enters its task through a shared wish to be silent side by side and to guard each other's solitude. In the evening Mr and Mrs Ramsay each read their own book, their eyes meet, neither wants to speak, "but something seemed, nevertheless, to go from him to her". "Don't interrupt me, he seemed to be saying, don't say anything; just sit there." **The Hermit at the main task is the same lighthouse up close**: solitude as daily work with a price of its own. The card does not change. The distance does.

report.h3: A twilight in which each fills in the other

report: Between the two Hermits lies The Moon — the night and the distance across the bay. Woolf finds the exact words for it: the two sit side by side, and she feels his mind "through the crepuscular walls of their intimacy". At dinner the lines he recites say "what had been in her mind the whole evening while she said different things".

report.h3: Two silences waiting for the first word

report: The main task is the same quiet on its minus side. In the decisive scene each silently asks for something different. She: "Say anything." He: just once, to hear that she loves him. Lisovskaya gives The Moon a piece of advice that fits this scene word for word: accept that a partner sometimes needs to sink into themselves; it does not mean they do not love. In the boat the father looks at the island in silence, and there is no knowing whether he is thinking "We perished, each alone" or "I have reached it. I have found it". report.h3: A shawl taken off without being asked

report: Woolf showed the way out as well. Mr Ramsay sees his wife alone and sad, and wants urgently to speak to her — but he resolves not to disturb her and passes by, "though it hurt him". And he would have passed, had she not "given him of her own free will what she knew he would never ask, and called to him and taken the green shawl off the picture frame, and gone to him". **He respects her solitude; she guesses his wish and steps out of her own quiet first.** Neither of them is wrong. All that matters is that someone stepped out.
The practice for a couple with this tail grows out of that same scene:

ul: to say what kind of quiet it is: "I need to be alone for a while — nothing is wrong between us";
to check guesses with a question rather than a silent conclusion;
to name small things while they are still small;
sometimes to step out first, without waiting to be asked;
to say simple things aloud: words of love, "well done", "I'm here". **Knowing and hearing are different things.**

unit.meaning: Your task is to step out of your own quiet first and say simple things aloud: knowing and hearing are different.
